title.en: Shaping of the Earth's surface: plate tectonics and landforms

text.en: The Earth's surface looks still, yet continents drift by a few centimetres every year. Over millions of years this slow movement builds mountains and opens oceans.

The Earth's surface is shaped by forces from inside, called endogenic, and forces from outside, called exogenic.
According to plate tectonics, the lithosphere is broken into large and small plates that move slowly over the softer layer below.
At plate boundaries plates may move apart, collide or slide past each other. These movements cause earthquakes, volcanoes and mountain building.
Landforms are natural features such as mountains, plateaus and plains. They are classified by height and shape.
Weathering breaks rocks, and erosion carries the pieces away by water, wind and ice. Deposition builds new landforms such as deltas.
Landforms influence where humans and other living beings live: rivers and plains support farming, and mountains support forests and pastoralism.
Disasters like earthquakes, landslides and volcanic eruptions can harm people, so preparedness matters.
Understanding landforms helps us plan settlements and protect lives.

problem.en: Explain how mountains form where two plates collide.

text.en: Two plates move towards each other.
Rocks between them are squeezed and folded upwards.
This slowly raises a mountain range like the Himalaya.

prompt.en: How do internal and external forces shape the Earth?

points.en: Plates of the lithosphere move slowly.
Plate movement causes earthquakes, volcanoes and mountains.
